notes.body: Knowledge has three layers, not two — outer, inner, and inner-of-the-inner. Picture an egg: the shell (visible exterior), the white (the protective layer beneath), and the yolk (the living core). Remove any one and it stops being an egg — life can't germinate. The three layers are a structural necessity, not poetic decoration.
notes.quote: the egg holds its shell, its white, and its golden heart

notes.body: Take the sentence 'the moon rose.' The name (moon), the attribute (rose), and the meaning (the actual disc in the sky) are three pillars, and none works alone: the disc with no name can't be communicated, the name with no disc is a hollow sound, the verb with no subject hangs in empty space. Religion has the same three layers — the words and acts, what they point to, and the divine reality beneath.

If the highest rung can't be handed over, what's the teacher for? He's a farmer: he fertilises the soil, plants the seed, waters, and pulls the weeds — he creates the perfect conditions. But he cannot force the green stalk up through the soil; germination happens invisibly inside the seed. The teacher tends; the teacher never transfers. The growing is entirely yours.
notes.anchor: the farmer cannot make the plant grow
notes.quote: But he cannot draw the green sprout out of the earth himself

notes.body: A good question to pose while reading: which rung in your own practice have you been treating as transferable — something a teacher or a book could just hand you — when the text insists it can only be earned by climbing?
notes.anchor: the highest rung cannot be transferred, only earned
notes.quote: is a station in which nothing avails except the work of its own people
